text: Every security team eventually writes the same formula on a whiteboard: risk equals likelihood times impact. It's the most common shorthand in the industry, and it's genuinely useful — but it also quietly misleads people who don't know what it's actually built to do. This lesson is about where that equation comes from, and three specific, well-documented ways it can fool you if you treat it as more than a triage tool.

The formal source is ISO 31000, the international risk management standard, which defines risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives — deliberately abstract, because it has to cover financial, safety, and project risk, not just cybersecurity. Security teams operationalize that with likelihood times impact, usually plotted on a five-by-five matrix that scores each from one to five and colors the result green, yellow, orange, or red. It's popular because it's fast: a risk committee can work through dozens of findings in an hour with no statistics background required.

But that speed hides three real problems. First, it flattens an entire range of possible loss outcomes into one point estimate, so a predictable medium-impact risk can look identical to one with a rare, catastrophic tail. Second, it scores every risk in isolation, missing the fact that several register entries often share one root cause — a single fix can retire more risk than the register shows. Third, likelihood and impact are usually informed guesses from whoever is in the room, not measured frequencies, and the equation doesn't distinguish a confident number from a shaky one.

Look at two risks that land on the same color band: one rare but catastrophic, scored two times five, and one frequent but moderate, scored four times three. Both multiply out to roughly the same number, and both might paint the same orange cell on the matrix. But they call for completely different treatment — one needs a plan for a bad tail event, the other needs day-to-day operational control. The matrix can't see that difference; a human reading only the color will miss it too.

None of this means the equation is broken — it means it's a triage tool, not a decision-grade financial model, and the mistake is using it for a six-figure investment decision instead of a quick ranking exercise. Next lesson draws that line precisely: when a fast qualitative score is genuinely the right call, and when the stakes justify switching to real quantitative numbers instead.
